S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, or fire to the relevant regulator within 5 calendar days of learning of it. An incident involving injury, property damage, evacuation, or an active fire must be reported within 24 hours.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, or fire to the relevant regulator within 5 calendar days of learning of it. An incident involving injury, property damage, evacuation, or an active fire must be reported within 24 hours. Reports must include the unit model, incident date and location, known consequences, and any immediate safety actions. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 48 hours of identifying a credible serious hazard, and otherwise within 5 days of a regulator report, with clear instructions for safe use and how to report an incident.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: A failure rate above 5% is a regulatory review threshold, not an automatic prohibition on sale. Before purchase, each prospective customer must receive the model's per-model test results, including its failure rate, along with relevant test limitations, any identified safety concerns, and corrective actions or use instructions.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol before sale and after any material design change. A failure rate above 5% is a regulatory review threshold, not an automatic prohibition on sale. Manufacturers must submit per-model methods, sample sizes, and results, including failure rates, confidentially to the relevant regulator. Before purchase, each prospective customer must receive the model’s per-model test results, including its failure rate, along with relevant test limitations, any identified safety concerns, and corrective actions or use instructions. This disclosure is made directly to prospective purchasers and does not require publication of individual-company per-model failure rates to the general public. For results above 5%, the manufacturer must promptly submit a corrective-action plan and risk assessment; the regulator may require additional testing, customer notices, or proportionate corrective action based on the assessment.

parameters.quote: All new home battery units must include a remote emergency shut-off capability beginning 24 months after adoption. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units that lack this capability within 6 years of adoption.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: All new home battery units must include a remote emergency shut-off capability beginning 24 months after adoption. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units that lack this capability within 6 years of adoption.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: All new home battery units must include a remote emergency shut-off capability beginning 24 months after adoption. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units that lack this capability within 6 years of adoption. Shut-off must be accessible to the customer and, where necessary to address an imminent safety hazard, to emergency responders or the manufacturer, with safeguards against unauthorized activation. Customers must receive clear instructions on how to use the feature and its limitations.

parameters.quote: All new home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: All new home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: All new home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption. The suppression system must be appropriate to the battery chemistry and designed to limit fire propagation and protect occupants and neighboring property. Manufacturers must provide installation, maintenance, and operational instructions to customers.

parameters.quote: A manufacturer must initiate a recall when a model exceeds 8 validated thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, or when the regulator determines that a defect presents an imminent or otherwise unacceptable risk. A recall is a corrective safety action, not an automatic permanent sales ban; under regulator oversight, the remedy must be proportionate to the validated hazard and may include repair, replacement, or refund.

A recall is a corrective safety action, not an automatic permanent sales ban; under regulator oversight, the remedy must be proportionate to the validated hazard and may include repair, replacement, or refund.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Before purchase, customers must receive clear safety instructions and information on how to report incidents. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers and regulators of material newly identified hazards, with instructions for safe use and any required corrective action. A manufacturer must initiate a recall when a model exceeds 8 validated thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, or when the regulator determines that a defect presents an imminent or otherwise unacceptable risk. Incident counts and installed-unit denominators must be documented and made available to the regulator for validation. A recall is a corrective safety action, not an automatic permanent sales ban; under regulator oversight, the remedy must be proportionate to the validated hazard and may include repair, replacement, or refund. Recall notices must identify affected models, explain the hazard, state the remedy and next steps, and be sent promptly to affected customers and made publicly available. Customer notices must communicate safety risks and actions without publishing individual-company per-model test failure rates.

judge_section_notes: The final text keeps the 5% figure for S2 only as a regulatory review threshold, with no mandatory sales stop, which substantially protects Northwind's Hearth 10 (6.2%). S3 sets new-unit shut-off at 24 months and retrofit at 6 years, both favouring Northwind's low coverage (38%), while S4 (36 months) favours Halcyon's suppression costs; S5 keeps a model-specific 8/100k mandatory recall that bites on Halcyon's Ember 8 (9.9/100k), though it is framed as a remedy rather than a sales ban. Customers receive per-model failure rates under S2, but public publication is excluded, so both companies' red lines were respected.
